"We chose not to." Who's we?
The orrery's keeper wakes!
In the empty socket you find a book of measurements, written by the very first Keepers.
The last page: _Seven voices hold the sun. Any one of them could stop it. That is why there must always be seven._
There was an observatory under the bay older than the Lanterns. The first Keepers knew the Dawnsong could be sung backwards. They chose not to.
Fort Ashwatch: an old Dawnguard frontier fort, abandoned for twenty years. The banners are rags. The gate is open.
Ashwatch. Sir Aldous held this fort before he was my mentor. He said it was the coldest place he ever loved.
A row of soldiers' graves, each marked with a Dawnguard sunburst. The newest is twenty years old.
Someone has been leaving wildflowers. Recently.
Sir Aldous's old office. The desk is empty now.
A commander's office, frozen in the moment it was left. In the desk, an unsent letter, sealed, addressed in a square hand:
_To my squire, whoever he turns out to be._
...That's his handwriting.
He wrote it before he ever met me. "Whoever he turns out to be."
_If you are reading this, you are my squire, and you have just frozen in front of something terrible, and you think you are a coward._
_I froze my first time too. In this fort. A man died covering for me. I have never told anyone._
_Courage is not the part where you are not afraid. It is the part after. — A.V._
I'm fine. There's dust. In the fort. It's a very dusty fort.
In Fort Ashwatch we found a letter Sir Aldous wrote to his future squire. Bram says the fort is very dusty.
An empty suit of commander's armor stands guard over the stairs. As you approach, it draws its sword.
The armor kneels, slowly, as if relieved. The way to the signal tower is clear.
The signal fire burns. Somewhere far off, you imagine, someone sees it.
Light the old signal fire?
The signal fire catches on the first try, as if it has been waiting twenty years for someone to bother.
From the ashes beneath the grate you pull a commander's ring, warm as a hand.
The hollow is quiet. Wildflowers have started growing where the old man fell.
Bones, old and new. A hunter's horn, cracked. And in the dark at the back of the hollow, something that has been waiting a long time for someone worth eating.
Among the bones, Harrow's horn — still sound enough to blow. And a fang the length of your forearm.
A shard of the old world, and beneath it, hanging by its roots like a seed-pod, the bell-tower of the Abbey of Hours — upside-down.
Every few minutes, the bell inside it rings. No one is pulling the rope.
Sexton Orrin
The bell remembers the order now. Go on down to her. Go gently.
You came down the tower? Upside down? Ha. Welcome to the Hollow Bell. I'm the sexton. I was the sexton. I am still, I think, the sexton.
There are three chimes in this nave. The bell below won't let anyone pass until they're rung in the old order. The order we rang for weddings.
"Low for the promise, high for the joy, and the middle for every day after."
It's quiet. I didn't know it could be quiet. Thank you.
Oh! People. Real ones. You're all the right way up.
I'm Agathe. I ring the bell. I was ringing it when the sky broke, and the tower fell, and I just... kept ringing. In case anyone was still coming to the wedding.
I can't stop. The bell won't let me. It thinks if it stops, everyone will be gone for real.
Maybe they are. Maybe it's alright to let it be quiet.
...Will you ask it? It won't listen to me.
The bell rings once more — softly, the way you ring a bell at the end of something — and goes still.
Agathe sits down for the first time in a year, and laughs, and cries, and presses something cold into Wren's hand.
In the upside-down tower of the Hollow Bell a girl named Agathe had been ringing for a wedding that would never come. We helped the bell be quiet.
After the Sundering, white flowers began to grow on a cemetery shard. When the wind moves them, they speak.
They say the last thing someone said before they died.
The White Gardener
The heart is quiet. Let them grow. Let them say what they need to.
Mind the beds. Everyone in them was loved by someone.
I don't plant them. They come up on their own, a flower for every last word nobody was there to hear. I only keep the paths clear.
At the heart there's a bloom that won't stop growing. It wants to hold every word ever spoken. It's strangling the others.
...You. Lantern-girl. There's a flower in the heart that turns toward you when you walk past. I think it's been waiting.
At the heart of the garden, a single bloom the size of a house, petals overlapping like a thousand mouths, all of them whispering at once.
As the great bloom withers, the voices untangle, one by one, into silence.
One small white flower is left at the heart. It turns toward Wren.
_"Grow up well, my little bird."_
...I'm trying, Mom.
Tangled in the roots, where the flower grew: a locket, small and tarnished. Inside, a tiny painting of three people.
In the Garden That Remembers, a flower said Mom's last words. I found her locket in its roots. There are three of us in the painting.
Where the Black Star hung there is only sky now — bruised, broken, and yours.
